catalog_quote: Yerisiam has both contrastive tone and vowel length. The tone-bearing unit is the mora, with short vowels counted as a single mora, long vowels counted as two moras, and diphthongs variably counted as one or two moras (see below). Two underlying tones may be associated with moras: high (H) and low (L). It follows that contour tones may be realized only as the sequences HL and LH on long vowels and bimoraic diphthongs. [...] Three groups of common tonal patterns can be identified. Pattern 1 consists of high tone throughout the word (H). new_statements.rule_in_words: Yerisiam is analysed as a word-tone language (underlying H and L linked to moras; three dominant lexical melodies H, H..L, L*H, the last treated as default/toneless) with contrastive vowel length; the author gives no synchronic word-stress rule. Stress is mentioned only historically: Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress is said to survive as vowel length on the historically penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (For the length-from-stress correlation: 24 of 70 etymologised words lack the expected long penult; kinship terms, pronouns, numeral 'four' flagged as likely contaminated.) NUSA 2017 fn 3 concedes some length/tone facts might be reanalysable as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word/root melodies from an 1802-item lexicon; tonal alternations with pronominal prefixes and the enclitic =tà discussed; analysis explicitly 'not a full-scale instrumental or phonological analysis' (2017: 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Yerisiam [ire] = Glottolog ires1239 (Kamholz spells it Yerisiam; Glottolog ref title uses 'Yeresiam'; older name Iresim). Data from Kamholz's own fieldwork (2010-2013) in the Yerisiam-speaking villages west of Nabire, southern Cenderawasih Bay; no dialect split reported.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Tonal phonology', sec. 5.3.2 Yerisiam (pp. 106-116): Yerisiam has contrastive tone (H, L; TBU = mora) and contrastive vowel length; three common word-tone patterns (H, HL, L*H; pattern 3 analysed as underlyingly toneless/default). No synchronic word-stress rule is given. Stress appears only diachronically: p. 109 'Yerisiam descends from a proto-language that had penultimate stress, with former stress surviving as vowel length'; sec. 5.4 p. 117 'Traces of former penultimate stress were found in Ma'ya, Moor, and Yerisiam.'

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2017. Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay. NUSA: Linguistic studies of languages in and around Indonesia 62: 7-39.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 Yerisiam (pp. 18-24) repeats the dissertation analysis nearly verbatim: contrastive tone (H/L on moras) plus vowel length; speakers produce tonal contrasts consistently (p. 9). Only stress remark is historical (p. 21): 'Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress straightforwardly accounts for this, with former stress surviving as vowel length.' Footnote 3 (p. 9) concedes that what is analysed as length or tone might in some cases be reanalysable as stress.
